questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning of Security' refers to.
questions.a: Security refers to the freedom from threats to core values and the safety of the state and its citizens; in international relations it mainly concerns the ability of states to protect their sovereignty, territorial integrity and citizens from external and internal dangers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning of Security'.
questions.a: Security is about the absence of threats to core values -- survival, independence and well-being -- and the measures states take to protect them.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning of Security' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Introduction: What is Security?

concepts.title: Traditional Concepts of Security: External Threats

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Traditional Concepts of Security: External Threats' refers to.
questions.a: Traditional external security concerns the dangers posed by other states, including military attack, war, and the erosion of sovereignty, against which states build armed forces, form alliances and pursue deterrence.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Traditional Concepts of Security: External Threats'.
questions.a: Traditional external security focuses on threats from other states -- war, aggression and territorial loss -- and the policies of deterrence, defence and alliance used to counter them.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Traditional Concepts of Security: External Threats' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Traditional Concepts of Security: External

concepts.title: Traditional Concepts of Security: Internal Threats

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Traditional Concepts of Security: Internal Threats' refers to.
questions.a: Internal security concerns threats to stability and order from within the state, such as separatist movements, civil war, insurgency, and domestic violence, which challenge the authority and territorial integrity of the government.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Traditional Concepts of Security: Internal Threats'.
questions.a: Internal security threats arise from within the state -- separatism, insurgency, civil war and communal violence -- and require police, intelligence and political solutions rather than external military action.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Traditional Concepts of Security: Internal Threats' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Traditional Concepts of Security: Internal

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Traditional Security Policies' refers to.
questions.a: Traditional security policies are the strategies states adopt to deal with external threats, principally deterrence (threat of retaliation), defence (military capability), and alliance (partnership with other states), along with the option of disarmament and arms control.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Traditional Security Policies'.
questions.a: The four main traditional security policies are deterrence, defence, alliance-building and arms control, each addressing the problem of war and external aggression in different ways.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Traditional Security Policies' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Traditional Security Policies

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Non-Traditional Threats: Terrorism' refers to.
questions.a: Terrorism is a non-traditional security threat in which political groups use violence against civilians to create fear and pressure governments, transcending national borders and requiring international cooperation to combat.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Non-Traditional Threats: Terrorism'.
questions.a: Terrorism targets civilians to spread fear for political ends; it is a transnational threat that cannot be solved by any one state alone and requires cooperative security measures.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Non-Traditional Threats: Terrorism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Non-Traditional Threats: Terrorism

concepts.title: Non-Traditional Threats: Poverty, Health and Migration

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Non-Traditional Threats: Poverty, Health and Migration' refers to.
questions.a: Poverty, health pandemics and migration are non-traditional security threats that endanger human well-being across borders, as economic deprivation, disease outbreaks and large population movements destabilise societies and require cooperative global responses.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Non-Traditional Threats: Poverty, Health and Migration'.
questions.a: Poverty, health and migration are non-traditional threats because they harm people rather than states directly, cross national borders and demand cooperative rather than purely military solutions.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Non-Traditional Threats: Poverty, Health and Migration' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Non-Traditional Threats: Poverty, Health and Migration

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cooperative Security' refers to.
questions.a: Cooperative security is an approach in which states work together through international organisations, alliances and multilateral frameworks to address both traditional and non-traditional threats that no single state can resolve alone.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cooperative Security'.
questions.a: Cooperative security recognises that many contemporary threats -- terrorism, pandemics, climate change -- are transnational and require collective action through international organisations rather than unilateral state action.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cooperative Security' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Cooperative Security

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Human Security' refers to.
questions.a: Human security is a concept that shifts the referent of security from the state to the individual, focusing on protecting people from threats such as poverty, hunger, disease, repression and environmental degradation, as proposed in the 1994 UN Human Development Report.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Human Security'.
questions.a: Human security broadens security beyond military threats to the state to include the safety and well-being of individuals from poverty, disease, repression and environmental harm.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Human Security' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Human Security

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India's Security Strategy' refers to.
questions.a: India's security strategy combines traditional military preparedness, internal security measures, economic development, democratic governance and nuclear deterrence to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and citizens from both external and internal threats.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India's Security Strategy'.
questions.a: India's security strategy is multi-dimensional, blending military strength, nuclear deterrence, economic development, democratic institutions and international cooperation to address both traditional and non-traditional threats.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India's Security Strategy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India's Security Strategy
